title: 2025 AMC 10A Problem 21
statement: A set of numbers is called sum-free if whenever \(x\) and \(y\) are (not necessarily distinct) elements of the set, \(x + y\) is not an element of the set. For example, \(\{1, 4, 6\}\) and the empty set are sum-free, but \(\{2, 4, 5\}\) is not. What is the greatest possible number of elements in a sum-free subset of \(\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 20\}?\)

solutions.text: We can reach \(10.\) The odds \(\{1, 3, 5, \ldots, 19\}\) are sum-free, since two odds sum to an even. So is \(\{11, 12, \ldots, 20\},\) since any two of those sum past \(20.\) Each has \(10\) elements. Now let \(m\) be the largest element of any sum-free subset. For \(1\le i<\frac{m}{2},\) at most one member of \(\{i,m-i\}\) can be chosen, because the two sum to \(m.\) If \(m\) is even, \(\frac{m}{2}\) cannot be chosen either, since it can be used twice and \(\frac{m}{2}+\frac{m}{2}=m.\) Thus besides \(m\) there are at most \(\lfloor\frac{m-1}{2}\rfloor\) chosen elements, for a total of at most \(\lfloor\frac{m-1}{2}\rfloor+1\le10.\) Therefore the greatest possible size is \(10.\) Thus, C is the correct answer.
hints: Both \(\{1, 3, 5, \ldots, 19\}\) and \(\{11, 12, \ldots, 20\}\) are sum-free, each with \(10\) elements
If \(m\) is the largest element, pair \(1\) to \(m-1\) as \(\{i, m-i\};\) each pair contributes at most one element
